rejected.title: Tourism on Country
card: Country is the word many Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use for the land, waters and sky they belong to and care for. It includes culture, law and family ties to place.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples run tours, art experiences and cultural centres. They choose which stories, places and practices to share, and how. This is sharing culture on their own terms.
Some places are sacred sites. Visitors are asked to respect them by following rules, staying on set paths and not entering or photographing restricted areas.
Uluru is one example. The Anangu, its Traditional Owners, asked visitors not to climb it, and the climb was closed in October 2019. Visitors can still walk around the base and join Anangu-led tours.
rejected.remember: Tourism on Country works best when Traditional Owners decide what is shared and visitors respect their wishes.

a.q: What does it mean for a tour to share culture on the terms of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples?
opts: The Traditional Owners choose what is shared and how
Visitors choose which stories and places they see
A tourism company decides which practices are shown
The tour shows every sacred site to all who pay
a.why: Sharing on their own terms means the Traditional Owners decide what is shared and how it is shared. Visitors choosing what they see is tempting, but it takes that decision away from the people who hold the culture.
a.clue: Think about who holds the knowledge and who makes the choice.

b.q: Jess is visiting a national park on Country. A sign says a nearby site is sacred and visitors must stay on the marked path. She wants a closer photo from off the path. What should she do?
opts: Stay on the path, as the Traditional Owners have asked
Go off the path, as the site is in a public park
Go off the path, as a photo does no harm
Ask other tourists whether it is fine to leave the path
b.why: Visitors are asked to respect sacred sites by following the rules set by the Traditional Owners. Being in a public park does not change this, because the rules protect a place that matters to the people of that Country.
b.clue: Who set the rule, and why?

version.title: Tourism on Country
card: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples run tours, art centres and cultural centres on their Country. Visitors learn about the land and its culture from the people whose Country it is.
They share culture on their own terms. The community decides which stories, places and practices visitors may learn about, and some knowledge is kept private.
Visitors are asked to respect sacred sites, places of deep cultural and spiritual meaning. This can mean staying on paths, keeping out of some areas and not taking photos.
Uluru is sacred to the Anangu, its Traditional Owners, who long asked visitors not to climb it. The climb closed in October 2019. Visitors can still walk around its base and join Anangu-led tours.
version.remember: The people of Country decide what culture is shared, and visitors respect sacred places.

a.q: An Aboriginal-run tour shows visitors some rock art, but the guide says the meaning of one site will not be shared. What does this show?
opts: The community is sharing culture on its own terms
The guide does not know the story of that site
The story has been lost, so it cannot be shared
The visitors chose which parts of culture to see
a.why: The community decides what visitors may learn, and some knowledge is kept private. A lost story is tempting, but the guide chose not to share it, which is different from not knowing it.
a.clue: Who decides what visitors may learn?

b.q: Sam is visiting Uluru-Kata Tjuta National Park and wants to see Uluru up close. Which plan respects the wishes of the Anangu?
opts: Walk around the base and join an Anangu-led tour
Climb early in the morning before many people arrive
Take photos of every site he passes on the base walk
Climb only part of the way up, then come back down
b.why: Walking around the base and joining an Anangu-led tour lets Sam see Uluru while respecting the Anangu. Photos of every site is tempting, but some sacred sites are not to be photographed.
b.clue: Which plan keeps Sam off the rock and follows the site rules?

a.best: The community is sharing culture on its own terms

b.best: Walk around the base and join an Anangu-led tour

check.summary: No problems found. The Uluru facts (Anangu as Traditional Owners, the climb closing in October 2019, base walks and Anangu-led tours, photography limits at some sacred sites) check out.
